claims.text: Local atomic-scale chemical disorder governs the onset of surface premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Local atomic-scale chemical disorder governs the overall melting temperature of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Variations in short-range order are associated with lattice strain in these nanoparticles.
Homogeneous elemental mixing produces higher cohesive surface energy than elemental clustering.
Homogeneously mixed nanoparticles resist premelting to a higher temperature than nanoparticles containing elemental clusters.
High-entropy alloys are commonly defined as containing five or more principal elements in near-equimolar proportions.
Rapid high-temperature synthesis ensures homogeneous elemental mixing in HEA nanoparticles.
Post-synthesis annealing can induce short-range elemental ordering or clustering in otherwise identical HEA nanoparticles.
Elemental clustering produces variations in lattice strain and surface bonding energies.
Uniform elemental mixing distributes bond strengths more evenly and raises the energy barrier for surface atomic disorder.
Elemental clusters create local weak spots that initiate surface premelting at lower temperatures.
Minimally clustered HEA nanoparticles will melt tens of degrees Celsius above comparable annealed, clustered nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship should hold for particles below 100 nm when configurational entropy dominates enthalpic segregation.
The proposed relationship may fail when large-scale phase separation or multiple phases form.
The magnitude of the premelting and melting-temperature shifts depends on particle size and elemental composition.
A statistically significant absence of lower premelting and melting temperatures in the clustered batch would falsify the stated directional hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The terminology conflates chemical disorder with short-range order and clustering. Homogeneous random mixing is ordinarily more chemically disordered, whereas annealing-induced short-range ordering reduces disorder; the hypothesis does not consistently specify whether increasing disorder, increasing order, or increasing clustering is the operative variable.
